summaries.example: Imagine a sentence such as “The red ball is on the table.” We can check whether it is true by looking at the ball and the table. Tarski wanted logic to explain this checking process carefully for formal languages. His idea was to describe when a sentence is true by looking at what its parts mean and how they fit together.
summaries.summary: Alfred Tarski was a mathematician and logician whose work made important ideas about language more precise. He developed a way to define truth for carefully built languages. The definition uses a related language that can talk about the first language. For a sentence to count as true, the definition must connect it with the way the sentence is translated or understood. Tarski also explained logical consequence by using interpretations, which are ways of assigning meanings to the non-logical signs in a language. A conclusion is a logical consequence of some premises when every interpretation that makes the premises true also makes the conclusion true. He studied which signs should count as logical constants. His later proposal said that a logical idea is one that stays unchanged when the objects in the world are rearranged one-to-one. Tarski’s work also showed why truth creates special difficulties when a language tries to talk about its own truth. The familiar liar-style puzzle can produce a contradiction, so Tarski separated the language being discussed from the language doing the discussing. This work helped shape modern logic and the study of meaning.
key_ideas: Tarski was a major twentieth-century logician who studied truth, logic, and mathematics.
He wanted definitions of truth that were exact enough for mathematical proofs.
His truth method connects a sentence with the conditions that make it true.
A logical conclusion should stay true under every allowed way of interpreting the important words.
Tarski showed that a language cannot, in a suitable general way, contain its own complete truth description without risking paradoxes.
summaries.why_it_matters: Tarski showed how careful definitions can turn everyday ideas into tools for mathematics and computer-like reasoning. His work helps people distinguish the words inside a language from the words used to describe that language. It also explains why some arguments work because of their form, not because of special facts about the subject. These ideas are important for understanding proofs, models, and the limits of formal systems.

important_terms.definition: A sentence or sign that says something about a subject, such as whether an object has a property.
A language made with carefully specified symbols and rules, often used in mathematics and logic.
A sentence is true when it matches the way things are, according to the intended meaning.
A sentence is a logical consequence when it must be true whenever certain starting sentences are true.
A larger language used to talk about another language and its sentences.

questions_to_think_about: How could you test whether a simple sentence is true?
Why might a language need another language to talk about itself safely?
What makes a conclusion follow from some starting statements?
Should words such as “and” and “all” count as logical words? Why?

summaries.example: Let K contain “Every number in the domain is not less than 0” and “0 is in the domain,” and let X be “0 is not less than 0.” The point of Tarski’s account is not merely that these particular words have their usual meanings. An interpretation may replace the non-logical symbols with other suitable objects or relations. X is a logical consequence of K only if every interpretation that makes all members of K true also makes X true. This makes consequence depend on truth preservation across interpretations, rather than on one intended subject matter alone.
summaries.summary: Alfred Tarski’s philosophical importance lies chiefly in his mathematical treatment of semantic notions: truth, satisfaction, logical consequence, and logicality. He sought definitions that could be formulated in accepted foundational systems rather than taking semantic concepts as unexplained primitives. For a formal language, satisfaction is defined recursively: atomic formulas are handled first, and the clauses for negation, connectives, and quantifiers determine the conditions for more complex formulas. Truth can then be defined through satisfaction, with a metalanguage proving appropriate sentence-by-sentence equivalences. Tarski’s requirement for an adequate truth definition is often summarized by Convention T: the metalanguage must support the connection between a sentence and the assertion expressed by that sentence. The separation between object language and metalanguage prevents the ordinary liar construction from applying directly to the defined truth predicate. Yet the separation also reveals a limit. For sufficiently expressive languages, a metalanguage no stronger than the object language cannot generally define a truth predicate satisfying the required conditions. Tarski’s theorem of the indefinability of truth uses a diagonal argument to establish this negative result. His theory of logical consequence shifts attention from syntactic derivation alone to semantic preservation. A conclusion follows logically from premises when every model of the premises is also a model of the conclusion. Tarski recognized that this definition presupposes a division between logical and extra-logical vocabulary. key_ideas: Tarski’s semantic project aimed to give mathematically rigorous definitions of truth, satisfaction, definability, and denotation for classical formal languages.
His Convention T requires a truth definition to support instances linking a sentence’s truth with the sentence itself, expressed in a suitable metalanguage.
The recursive definition of satisfaction handles atomic formulas first and then extends to negation, connectives, and quantifiers.
The liar paradox is blocked because a Tarskian truth predicate is assigned to an object language from a stronger, distinct metalanguage.
Tarski’s account of consequence uses models and truth preservation under all permitted interpretations, not merely uniform replacement of existing symbols.
His later invariance proposal treats a notion as logical when it remains fixed under every one-to-one rearrangement of the underlying domain, while the result can depend on the formal context.
summaries.why_it_matters: Tarski’s distinctions organize several central questions in philosophy of language and logic. They explain how truth can be defined rigorously for formal systems, why self-reference can generate paradox, and why semantic consequence is not identical to derivability from a selected proof system. His work also connects model theory with philosophical questions about meaning and logical form. The invariance account of logical constants continues to focus attention on whether logicality is absolute or depends partly on the language and investigative context.

important_terms.definition: A precisely specified system of symbols, formation rules, and often a deductive system.
A language used to describe the expressions, interpretations, and truth conditions of an object language.
A relation between a formula and an assignment of objects to its variables; it is defined recursively from the formula’s structure.
A sentence is true, in a Tarskian treatment, when the relevant semantic conditions make it hold in the intended framework.
A sentence X is a logical consequence of K when every interpretation that models all sentences in K also models X.
An interpretation that makes a sentence, or every sentence in a set, true.
A symbol whose interpretation is kept fixed across the relevant reinterpretations, such as a quantifier or connective; the boundary is not always absolute.
The result that, for sufficiently expressive languages, truth cannot generally be defined within that same language without creating serious limitations.

questions_to_think_about: Why does defining truth for a language require distinguishing object language from metalanguage?
Is preserving truth under every interpretation stronger than preserving truth under substitutions using only the language’s available names?
Why can a language have a truth predicate for a simpler language but fail to define its own truth predicate?
Does invariance under every permutation provide a convincing test for logicality?
How might the choice of logical constants change what counts as a logical consequence?

summaries.example: Suppose a mystery club uses the rules: “Every club badge is marked with a star” and “Mina’s badge is a club badge.” The club concludes, “Mina’s badge is marked with a star.” This looks like a logical conclusion because the conclusion remains true whenever the two starting claims are true. Now replace “badge,” “club,” and “star” with other suitable meanings. Tarski’s idea is that a logical conclusion should still preserve truth under these changes, not just under the original story.
summaries.summary: Alfred Tarski was one of the most important logicians of the twentieth century. The SEP entry focuses on his work concerning truth, logical consequence, and logical constants. Tarski was interested in concepts that mathematicians used but had not yet defined with enough precision for foundational work. He developed a method for defining truth in classical formal languages. The method begins with satisfaction: a formula is satisfied when an assignment of objects to its variables fits the formula’s structure. Atomic formulas receive basic conditions, and more complicated formulas are handled using rules for negation, connectives, and quantifiers. Truth can then be described in a metalanguage, a language used to talk about the object language. An adequate definition must connect a sentence with what that sentence says, in the appropriate metalanguage. This arrangement also helps avoid the liar paradox. A truth predicate for the object language belongs to the metalanguage, so the object language cannot simply use that predicate to describe its own sentences. Tarski also proved a major limitation: for sufficiently expressive languages, truth cannot generally be defined inside the same language by the required method. On logical consequence, Tarski argued that syntactic proof rules do not capture every intuitive case. His semantic proposal says that a conclusion follows from premises when every model of the premises is a model of the conclusion. He later explored logical constants through invariance: a logical notion should remain unchanged under every one-to-one rearrangement of the underlying domain. The entry also notes that what counts as logical may vary with the formal context.
key_ideas: Tarski made the study of truth precise by defining it for formal languages rather than leaving it as an unexplained idea.
His method builds truth from satisfaction: first explain when formulas are satisfied, then explain when whole sentences are true.
The liar puzzle shows a danger in allowing a language to speak about its own truth in an unrestricted way.
Logical consequence is about preserving truth through all interpretations, not only about deriving a conclusion by familiar rules.
Tarski questioned whether the difference between logical and non-logical words is fixed forever or can depend on the language being studied.
He suggested that logical notions are those that remain unchanged when the domain is rearranged one-to-one.
summaries.why_it_matters: Tarski’s work gives students a map of several major ideas in modern logic. It shows how meaning can be studied with mathematical precision, why self-reference can be dangerous, and why an argument’s validity should not depend on the accidental subject matter of its words. His approach to models and interpretations is central to understanding how formal theories are evaluated. His discussion of logical constants also raises a continuing philosophical question: what makes a part of language genuinely logical?

important_terms.definition: A carefully constructed language with exact rules for making sentences and, often, for proving them.
A way of giving meanings to the non-logical signs of a formal language.
An interpretation that makes a sentence or group of sentences true.
The relation between a formula and the objects assigned to its variables; it helps explain when the formula is true.
A sentence that must be true whenever a given set of sentences is true, under every allowed interpretation.
The language used to explain an object language, including its symbols, sentences, and truth conditions.
A symbol treated as logical rather than as a term about a particular subject, though the boundary can depend on context.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a definition of truth need to talk about a sentence from outside that sentence’s own language?
Can a conclusion be logically correct even when it is about a surprising subject?
What is the difference between changing the meanings of words and changing the logical structure of an argument?
Why could a relation such as membership be logical in one formal setting but non-logical in another?
What problems might arise if a language tried to include a complete account of its own truth?
